name: Soil Erosion
description: Soil erosion removes and redistributes surface material through water and wind, connecting the condition of Iran’s hillslopes, agricultural land, and drylands. Regional research demonstrates why erosion maps, model estimates, and direct measurements must be interpreted differently.

seo.title: Soil Erosion in Iran: Processes, Evidence and Conservation | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand water and wind erosion in Iran, regional research, the limits of erosion estimates, and the importance of protecting soil cover.

content.heading: A moving surface
content.content:
Soil erosion is the removal and transport of soil by water or wind. It can occur naturally, but disturbance of protective vegetation can accelerate losses beyond the rate at which soil develops. Leaves, grass, plant litter, and roots protect the surface in different ways: they soften raindrop impacts, hold material together, and reduce exposure to moving air and water. Erosion therefore concerns the condition of the ground as much as the strength of a storm. [s1]

For understanding Iran, this distinction matters because a dry landscape can experience both wind erosion and erosion during rainfall. Little annual rain does not mean that runoff is harmless. The relevant questions include how intensely rain falls, whether the surface is protected, and how water moves across a slope. FAO identifies rainfall, soil susceptibility, land cover, management, and slope characteristics as interacting controls on water-erosion risk. [s2]

content.heading: Different processes require different evidence
content.content:
Water erosion involves detachment, transport, and eventual deposition. Rain and runoff loosen particles; flowing water moves them downslope; sediment then accumulates elsewhere. The effects can extend beyond the field or hillside where the loss began. Gullies and ravines alter the land surface, while sediment carried downhill can contribute to the silting of dams. A visibly eroded slope and a sediment-filled water body are connected parts of a landscape, although their measurements describe different things. [s1][s2]

Research in Rutak, in the Saravan area of southeastern Iran’s Baluchistan region, illustrates another approach. A study published in 2024 used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to classify land degradation in an area affected by wind erosion. The researchers compared combinations of surface reflectance and vegetation indices with field observations. Some combinations agreed better with field evidence than others. The important lesson is methodological: a satellite-derived degradation class is an assessment of surface conditions, rather than a direct weighing of soil removed each year. [s3]

content.heading: Reading erosion estimates carefully
content.content:
A separate central-Iran study applied the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation, or RUSLE, alongside climate-model scenarios. Its historical analysis considered selected years, while its future results depended on specified climate scenarios. Such work helps investigate where erosion may occur and how conditions could change. It does not establish a continuously measured national annual series, and projected outcomes should not be described as completed developments. [s4]

These distinctions shape conservation reporting. A convincing account should identify whether it describes water or wind erosion, the study boundary, the observation period, and the method used. The Rutak research also shows why field checks matter when satellite indicators are used to prioritize degraded land. Protecting vegetation addresses an important physical control, but claims that a particular intervention succeeded require evidence of outcomes at the relevant site. Iran’s erosion problem is best understood through clearly defined regional evidence, rather than a single unqualified national ranking. [s1][s3][s4]

name: Mountains & Highlands
description: Iran’s mountains organize contrasts between the Caspian shore, the interior plateau, and the country’s western and southern landscapes. The Alborz and Zagros reveal different combinations of relief, climate, rock structure, and drainage, while individual summits require their own geological accounts.

seo.title: Iran’s Mountains and Highlands: Alborz, Zagros and Beyond | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore how Iran’s mountains shape rainfall, drainage and landscapes, from the Alborz barrier to folded Zagros ridges and volcanic summits.

content.heading: More than a collection of summits
content.content:
Iran’s mountain geography is easiest to understand through contrasts between slopes, valleys, and adjoining lowlands. In the north, the Alborz separates the Caspian depression from the elevated interior. Its northern and southern sides differ sharply in climate and landscape. In the Zagros, satellite-derived relief reveals repeated ridges and intervening valleys, expressing the folding of layered rocks. These are distinct mountain settings, rather than interchangeable examples of high ground. [s1][s3]

A useful guide therefore asks several questions alongside the name of a peak: which mountain system contains it, what rocks and structures shape it, which direction its slopes face, and where its water drains. This approach connects the individual summit pages in this branch with the wider geography of Iran. The contrast between a volcanic cone such as Damavand and folded sedimentary terrain in the Zagros is particularly instructive. [s3][s5]

content.heading: The Alborz: a barrier with contrasting sides
content.content:
The Alborz forms the central section of Iran’s northern mountain arc. Its relief separates the Caspian lowlands from the central uplands, creating an important ecological boundary. The Sefidrud valley marks a major break toward its western end, while the range connects eastward with the mountains of Khorasan. Within it, high massifs, deep valleys, and passes make a more intricate landscape than the outline of a single continuous ridge suggests. [s1]

The range also contains different kinds of high mountain scenery. The Takht-e Solayman massif includes Alam Kuh, while Damavand rises as a volcanic cone in the central Alborz. Their shared regional setting does not make their landforms geologically equivalent. A range-wide overview establishes their position; the individual mountain pages examine what distinguishes each place. [s1][s5]

content.heading: The Zagros: folding made visible
content.content:
In the Zagros, the approach of Arabia toward Asia compresses the crust and folds sedimentary layers. NASA’s Shuttle Radar Topography Mission imagery shows upward-arching folds, called anticlines, and intervening downward folds, called synclines. Erosion exposes these structures unevenly because different rock layers resist removal differently. The resulting patterns explain why a relief map can appear as a sequence of elongated ridges rather than isolated cones. [s3]

Salt adds another distinctive process in parts of southern Iran. Buried salt can rise through overlying rocks and emerge at the surface. Where it spreads downslope, it forms features commonly called salt glaciers. The name describes their flowing shape; the moving material is salt. These formations show why the geology beneath a mountain landscape matters as much as its visible outline. Folded rocks, erosion, and mobile salt can operate together, producing terrain that a simple elevation ranking would not explain. [s4]

content.heading: Why exposure matters
content.content:
Mountain barriers redistribute moisture. Air approaching exposed slopes can produce precipitation, while sheltered terrain farther inland is drier. The northern Alborz flanks and western Zagros slopes are important examples of relatively well-watered mountain margins. Moving across a ridge can therefore mean crossing an ecological boundary as well as gaining or losing altitude. [s2]

Seasonality matters too. Snow stores part of the cold-season precipitation in mountain areas and releases water during melting. The historical climatic synthesis in Encyclopaedia Iranica connects this seasonal release with streams, groundwater, and cultivation. It provides a useful explanation of the physical relationship, rather than a measurement of present-day snow reserves. [s2]

content.content:

content.summary: The arrows describe a general climatic and hydrological relationship. They do not quantify rainfall, snow storage, or the contribution of any particular mountain to a river.

content.heading: From regional systems to individual places
content.content: This branch brings together Damavand, Alam Kuh, Sabalan, Zard Kuh, and Dena, alongside a comparison of the Alborz and Zagros ranges. It is best explored at two scales: mountain systems explain broad spatial relationships, while individual pages examine specific landforms and evidence. The same distinction should guide interpretation of maps and photographs. A snow-covered summit, a folded ridge, and an exposed salt flow may all belong to Iran’s highlands, but they reveal different processes. [s1][s3][s4][s5]

name: Damavand
description: Damavand is Iran’s highest mountain, a stratovolcano in the Alborz northeast of Tehran. Its lava-built slopes, summit fumaroles, and thermal springs reveal a volcanic history that extends beyond its familiar snow-covered silhouette.

seo.title: Damavand: Iran’s Highest Mountain and Its Volcanic History | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Damavand’s volcanic landforms, dated eruption evidence, thermal activity, differing elevation figures and UNESCO Tentative List record.

content.heading: Iran’s highest mountain
content.content:
Damavand rises within the Alborz mountain range northeast of Tehran. It is Iran’s highest mountain and a stratovolcano: a volcanic edifice built through successive eruptions. Its setting combines the regional geography of a mountain chain with the distinct form of an individual volcano. NASA’s astronaut-photography account shows how snow can emphasize solidified lava flows on the western flank, making parts of that eruptive history visible from space. [s1]

Published elevations require care. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program lists 5,670 metres, whereas Iran’s UNESCO Tentative List submission gives approximately 5,628 metres. NASA’s page itself contains both figures in different passages. These sources establish Damavand’s exceptional height but do not resolve the measurement discrepancy. The figures should be attributed to their sources rather than presented as evidence of a change in the mountain’s elevation. [s1][s2][s3]

content.heading: A cone built over a longer history
content.content:
The Global Volcanism Program describes a younger cone constructed over an older volcanic edifice. Activity was concentrated mainly at the summit, sending lava flows outward across the slopes. Its geological summary places construction of the younger cone within roughly the past 600,000 years, a much longer history than the recent lava surfaces alone might suggest. [s2]

The database records a confirmed eruptive period at approximately 5350 BCE, with an uncertainty of 200 years, based on uranium-series isotopic evidence. This is a geological age estimate, not a dated eyewitness account. No historically recorded eruptions are identified in the profile. Keeping those categories separate avoids turning an approximate prehistoric date into an artificially precise historical event. [s2]

content.heading: Quiet does not mean thermally inactive
content.content:
Hot springs occur on Damavand’s flanks, and fumaroles—vents that release volcanic gases and steam—have been documented near the summit crater. NASA interprets these features as evidence for a hot or cooling body of magma beneath the volcano and describes Damavand as dormant rather than extinct. This is a geological explanation, not a forecast of an eruption. [s1]

The Smithsonian profile includes summit observations from 1993 and 1999, including sulfur deposits and fumarolic activity. Those reports document conditions during particular visits. They should not be repurposed as a current gas-emission survey or evidence of newly developing unrest. [s2]

content.heading: A heritage proposal with defined limits
content.content:
Iran submitted Damavand to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 5 February 2008. The submission emphasizes thermal springs, plant communities, and endemic flora. A Tentative List entry records a state’s proposed heritage property; it is not itself World Heritage inscription. UNESCO also makes clear that responsibility for the entry’s content rests with the submitting state. [s3]

This distinction matters when describing the surrounding environment. The submission provides evidence of the values Iran advanced for recognition, while detailed claims about present biodiversity or conservation effectiveness require additional ecological research. Damavand can therefore be understood through complementary records: volcanic research explains its construction and thermal features, imagery reveals landforms, and the heritage submission documents an institutional proposal. [s1][s2][s3]
